analysis.one_liner: Cuts PAC contribution limits, restricts House campaign donations to local residents, and gives challengers free mailings.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, so PAC contribution limits and incumbent fundraising advantages stayed unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal campaign finance rules for House elections. It cuts the maximum a political action committee can give a candidate from $5,000 to $2,000, bars House candidates from taking money from anyone outside their state, and requires that donations from outside the candidate's own district not exceed donations from inside it. It also gives challengers running against an incumbent two free taxpayer-paid mailings to district voters, limited to biography and platform statements.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want congressional campaigns funded more by local residents and less by political action committees and out-of-district money. Nonincumbent challengers gain a communication tool to counter the incumbent's free use of the congressional franking privilege, and their donors inside the district would carry relatively more weight.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the ceiling on what multicandidate political committees (PACs) may contribute to a candidate from $5,000 to $2,000, reducing the weight of organized money in House races.

Prohibits House candidates from accepting contributions from anyone who is not an individual resident of the state holding the election, and requires that out-of-district contributions not exceed in-district contributions, shifting influence toward the voters the candidate would actually represent.

Gives nonincumbent candidates two free bulk-rate mass mailings to district residents, funded from the House's official mail allowance, to offset the incumbent's ability to mail constituents at government expense; the mailings are limited to biographical and platform statements and must go out no later than 60 days before the election.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees and organized interest groups lose half of their per-candidate giving power. Incumbent House members lose a fundraising and financial edge over challengers, and donors outside the district or state lose the ability to give at all. Taxpayers bear the small cost of the challengers' mailings through the House official mail allowance.

drawbacks.text: The free mailings are paid from the House's official mail allowance, meaning taxpayers directly finance part of challengers' campaign communications, and the bill authorizes this only in races where an incumbent is running.

The ban on contributions from non-residents and the limits on mailing content restrict political speech and participation, raising First Amendment-style objections that courts have often applied to campaign finance rules.
The in-district versus out-of-district matching rule is mechanically complex to enforce and does not cap total individual contribution amounts, so well-funded in-district donors could still dominate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real problems — heavy PAC money, out-of-district donations, and the incumbent's free-mailing advantage — with modest, narrow tools. Its costs are small and mostly borne by organized interest groups and incumbents, though the taxpayer-funded challenger mailings and the speech restrictions are legitimate design concerns. It would not have transformed campaign finance; it would have nudged House races slightly toward local voters and challengers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Administration Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Nancy Johnson introduced the bill on October 16, 1991, during the first session of the 102nd Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on House Administration the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it.
No committee vote, floor debate, or roll-call vote ever occurred, and with the 102nd Congress ending on January 3, 1993, the bill expired without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and political action committees kept the existing rules: PACs retained the $5,000 per-election contribution ceiling, outside-district and out-of-state donors kept full access, and challengers gained no free-mailing counterweight.

for.name: Rep. Nancy L. Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Citizens Election Campaign Campaign Reform Act on October 16, 1991.

for.name: Two House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan voting pattern exists; the record shows only a one-party sponsorship team.

industries.note: Their per-candidate contribution ceiling would drop from $5,000 to $2,000, halving organized interest groups' direct giving power in House races. Ordinary voters gain influence relative to organized money.
Incumbents benefit from PAC money, out-of-district donations, and free official mailings to constituents; the bill trims all three advantages and hands challengers two free mailings of their own.
Non-residents of the state could no longer contribute at all, and donors outside the district could give no more than in-district donors combined, concentrating influence with local voters.
